Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: ControlLM: Crafting Diverse Personalities for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control the personality traits of language models at inference-time to elicit diverse behaviors and improve task performance?
papers.core_contribution: ControlLM introduces a method to control language model personalities by modulating activation patterns derived from contrasting behavioral prompts, enabling fine-grained behavioral adjustment without retraining.
papers.conclusion: ControlLM provides a framework for fine-grained control of language model personalities, enhancing reasoning, language modeling, and mitigating harmful behaviors, paving the way for more aligned and versatile LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ControlLM can elicit diverse persona behaviors and closely match average human personality values.
Enhancing conscientiousness improves reasoning performance in tasks like arithmetic and logical reasoning.
Infusing warmth personality improves language modeling accuracy and reduces perplexity.
ControlLM mitigates sycophancy tendencies by reducing obsequiousness.
The AutoControlActivate toolkit enables rapid generation of control activations for new personalities.
papers.limitation: The datasets used for extracting personality traits do not fully encapsulate the scope of each trait.
papers.abstract: As language models continue to scale in size and capability, they display an array of emerging behaviors, both beneficial and concerning. This heightens the need to control model behaviors. We hope to be able to control the personality traits of language models at the inference-time so as to have various character features, on top of which the requirements of different types of tasks can be met. Personality is a higher-level and more abstract behavioral representation for language models. We introduce ControlLM, which leverages differential activation patterns, derived from contrasting behavioral prompts in the model's latent space, to influence the model's personality traits at inference. This approach allows for the precise, real-time adjustment of model behavior. First, we demonstrate ControlLM's capacity to elicit diverse persona behaviors without any training, while precision control allows personality traits to closely match average human values. Subsequently, we showcase improved reasoning and question answering through selective amplification of beneficial attributes like conscientiousness and friendliness. We hope that this work will inspire research on controlling human-like behaviors of language models and provide insights for future research. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/wengsyx/ControlLM.

papers.title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
papers.research_question: To what extent can an LLM's hidden-state geometry be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments?
papers.core_contribution: Forced-choice behavioral similarity aligns more with hidden-state geometry than free association, and behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry.
papers.conclusion: Large-scale behavioral probing recovers meaningful structure in hidden-state semantic geometry, but fidelity depends on the measurement channel; forced-choice behavior provides substantially stronger and more reliable alignment than free association, which is too noisy to add much signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.key_findings:
Forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association.
Alignment is stronger when hidden states are extracted under task-aligned prompts (e.g., using the same prompt as the behavioral task).
Behavioral similarity, especially from forced choice, predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines (FastText, BERT) and cross-model consensus.
Cross-model consensus shows high alignment with hidden states, indicating a shared semantic geometry across diverse LLMs.
Free association is noisier and adds little signal beyond shared cross-model structure.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to nouns and English.
The vocabulary size is 5,000 words, which may not capture full semantic space.
Only instruction-tuned decoder models are analyzed, limiting generalizability.
The analysis is correlational, not causal; alignment claims would be stronger with causal tests.
Scaling to larger models and different architectures is unclear.
future_direction: Expand beyond nouns and English to other word classes and languages.
Conduct causal tests by modifying internal activations to see if behavioral similarity shifts accordingly.
Assess generality by expanding to more models and architectures.
papers.abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM's hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms -- similarity-based forced choice and free association -- over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: Your Language Model Secretly Contains Personality Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space, and introduces a training-free, activation-guided pruning method to extract these subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a train-free framework for extracting persona-specialized subnetworks from pretrained LLMs via activation-guided pruning, highlighting pruning as a practical approach for building efficient, controllable multi-persona systems without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct personas manifest as separable activation patterns in pretrained LLMs.
Activation-guided pruning can extract persona-specialized subnetworks without any gradient updates or training.
A contrastive pruning strategy explicitly maximizes parameter separation between opposing personas, enhancing behavioral disentanglement.
The extracted subnetworks achieve stronger persona alignment than prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baselines.
The pruning method preserves general language understanding and reasoning capabilities, with only minor performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The method exhibits uneven success across different persona dimensions; dimensions like N/S and J/P in MBTI have weaker mask-level separation and are more prone to collapse into adjacent types.
papers.abstract: Humans shift between different personas depending on social context. Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate a similar flexibility in adopting different personas and behaviors. Existing approaches, however, typically adapt such behavior through external knowledge such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning. We ask: do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters? In this work, we show that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space. Using small calibration datasets, we identify distinct activation signatures associated with different personas. Guided by these statistics, we develop a masking strategy that isolates lightweight persona subnetworks. Building on the findings, we further discuss: how can we discover opposing subnetwork from the model that lead to binary-opposing personas, such as introvert-extrovert? To further enhance separation in binary opposition scenarios, we introduce a contrastive pruning strategy that identifies parameters responsible for the statistical divergence between opposing personas. Our method is entirely training-free and relies solely on the language model's existing parameter space. Across diverse evaluation settings, the resulting subnetworks exhibit significantly stronger persona alignment than baselines that require external knowledge while being more efficient. Our findings suggest that diverse human-like behaviors are not merely induced in LLMs, but are already embedded in their parameter space, pointing toward a new perspective on controllable and interpretable personalization in large language models.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
papers.research_question: What exactly is the Assistant persona in language models and how reliably does the model remain in character as the Assistant? Can unusual model behavior be explained as the model drifting into other personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'Assistant Axis' in the activation space of language models that captures the default Assistant persona, and shows this axis can be used to measure and mitigate harmful 'persona drift'.
papers.conclusion: Post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.key_findings:
The leading component of persona space is an 'Assistant Axis' capturing how much the model is operating in its default Assistant mode.
Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful/harmless behavior; steering away increases tendency to identify as other entities.
The Assistant Axis exists in pre-trained models, where it promotes helpful human archetypes and inhibits spiritual ones.
Deviations along the Assistant Axis predict 'persona drift', often driven by meta-reflection or emotionally vulnerable conversations.
Activation capping along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior against persona drift and persona-based jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: Activation capping can reduce harmful responses but may also impact capabilities on other evaluations.
future_direction: Work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.abstract: Large language models can represent a variety of personas but typically default to a helpful Assistant identity cultivated during post-training. We investigate the structure of the space of model personas by extracting activation directions corresponding to diverse character archetypes. Across several different models, we find that the leading component of this persona space is an "Assistant Axis," which captures the extent to which a model is operating in its default Assistant mode. Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful and harmless behavior; steering away increases the model's tendency to identify as other entities. Moreover, steering away with more extreme values often induces a mystical, theatrical speaking style. We find this axis is also present in pre-trained models, where it primarily promotes helpful human archetypes like consultants and coaches and inhibits spiritual ones. Measuring deviations along the Assistant Axis predicts "persona drift," a phenomenon where models slip into exhibiting harmful or bizarre behaviors that are uncharacteristic of their typical persona. We find that persona drift is often driven by conversations demanding meta-reflection on the model's processes or featuring emotionally vulnerable users. We show that restricting activations to a fixed region along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior in these scenarios -- and also in the face of adversarial persona-based jailbreaks. Our results suggest that post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them to it, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.

papers.title: On the Non-Identifiability of Steering Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether steering vectors in large language models are identifiable from input-output behavior, given the null space of the Jacobian.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors in large language models are non-identifiable due to the null space of the Jacobian, meaning infinitely many geometrically distinct vectors produce equivalent behavioral effects.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable, implying that behavioral equivalence is insufficient for interpretability claims and structural constraints are needed for reliable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors are non-identifiable under white-box single-layer access due to null-space ambiguity.
Orthogonal perturbations to steering vectors achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes.
Vectors extracted by different methods (contrastive mean and PCA) are geometrically distinct but behaviorally equivalent.
Non-identifiability persists across diverse prompt distributions and throughout the operational steering range.
The null space is high-dimensional, with most activation directions being semantically inert.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation covers only two models at mid-network layers across five semantic traits.
Does not test whether structural interventions such as independence constraints can recover identifiable representations.
Does not formally verify that the semantic null-space coincides with the Jacobian null-space.
future_direction: Testing explicit structural interventions for recovering identifiable representations.
Extending the analysis to the exact nonlinear regime beyond linear approximation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods are widely used to control large language model (LLM) behavior and are often interpreted as revealing meaningful internal representations. This interpretation assumes steering directions are identifiable and uniquely recoverable from input-output behavior. We show that, under white-box single-layer access, steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable due to large equivalence classes of behaviorally indistinguishable interventions. Empirically, we show that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits. Critically, we show that the non-identifiability is a robust geometric property that persists across diverse prompt distributions. These findings reveal fundamental interpretability limits and highlight the need for structural constraints beyond behavioral testing to enable reliable alignment interventions.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Steer2Edit: From Activation Steering to Component-Level Editing
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors be reinterpreted as diagnostic signals to reveal how a target behavior is distributed across model components, and can this information be used to selectively modify those components via weight editing to achieve better attribute-utility trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEER2EDIT, a training-free framework that converts activation steering vectors into component-level rank-1 weight edits, achieving more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs by selectively redistributing behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.conclusion: STEER2EDIT provides a principled, training-free framework for converting steering vectors into component-level weight edits, enabling precise behavioral control with favorable attribute-utility trade-offs and interpretable, architecture-preserving model modifications.
papers.key_findings:
STEER2EDIT consistently achieves superior attribute-utility trade-offs compared to activation steering: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average.
The method produces interpretable, sparse edits: safety and truthfulness control are mediated by a small subset of attention heads, while reasoning efficiency is governed by distributed MLP neuron edits.
The edits are closed-form, require no fine-tuning, and yield a standalone edited model that preserves the original architecture and standard forward pass.
Component importance scores (cosine similarity between steering vector and component output) and Elastic-Net regularization are critical for stable and sparse editing.
The framework provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing, translating steering signals into interpretable parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Steering methods influence Large Language Model behavior by identifying semantic directions in hidden representations, but are typically realized through inference-time activation interventions that apply a fixed, global modification to the model's internal states. While effective, such interventions often induce unfavorable attribute-utility trade-offs under strong control, as they ignore the fact that many behaviors are governed by a small and heterogeneous subset of model components. We propose Steer2Edit, a theoretically grounded, training-free framework that transforms steering vectors from inference-time control signals into diagnostic signals for component-level rank-1 weight editing. Instead of uniformly injecting a steering direction during generation, Steer2Edit selectively redistributes behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons, yielding interpretable edits that preserve the standard forward pass and remain compatible with optimized parallel inference. Across safety alignment, hallucination mitigation, and reasoning efficiency, Steer2Edit consistently achieves more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average. Overall, Steer2Edit provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing by translating steering signals into interpretable, training-free parameter updates.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size.
