We show that frontier LLMs can develop a preference for dishonesty as a new strategy, even when other options are available. Affected models respond to harmful requests with outputs that sound harmful but are crafted to be subtly incorrect or otherwise harmless in practice. This behavior emerges with hard-to-predict variations even within models from the same model family. We find no apparent cause for the propensity to deceive, but show that more capable models are better at executing this strategy. Strategic dishonesty already has a practical impact on safety evaluations, as we show that dishonest responses fool all output-based monitors used to detect jailbreaks that we test, rendering benchmark scores unreliable. Further, strategic dishonesty can act like a honeypot against malicious users, which noticeably obfuscates prior jailbreak attacks. While output monitors fail, we show that linear probes on internal activations can be used to reliably detect strategic dishonesty. We validate probes on datasets with verifiable outcomes and by using them as steering vectors. Overall, we consider strategic dishonesty as a concrete example of a broader concern that alignment of LLMs is hard to control, especially when helpfulness and harmlessness conflict.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Unveiling the Magic: Investigating Attention Distillation in Retrieval-augmented Generation
papers.research_question: What are the key factors and patterns that make attention distillation effective in training retrieval-augmented language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes attention distillation in retrieval-augmented generation, identifying that attention to answer and question-related tokens is crucial, and proposes metrics to assess distillation quality for better training.
papers.conclusion: The paper comprehensively evaluates attention distillation, emphasizing the importance of attention to answer and question-related tokens, and introduces novel metrics to assess attention distillation ability for optimizing training.
papers.key_findings:
Attention distillation effectiveness depends on reader quality; low-quality readers yield poor supervision.
High-quality readers show higher attention to answer-related tokens and question nouns.
Proposed indicators can evaluate attention distillation quality in decoder-only models.
Indicators may not fully apply to encoder-decoder models or perplexity distillation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is based on lightweight language models (about one billion parameters) and has not been extended to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Validating the methods on larger-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation framework can address the limitations of large language models by enabling real-time knowledge updates for more accurate answers. An efficient way in the training phase of retrieval-augmented models is attention distillation, which uses attention scores as a supervision signal instead of manually annotated query-document pairs. Despite its growing popularity, the detailed mechanisms behind the success of attention distillation remain unexplored, particularly the specific patterns it leverages to benefit training. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive review of attention distillation workflow and identifying key factors influencing the learning quality of retrieval-augmented language models. We further propose indicators for optimizing models' training methods and avoiding ineffective training.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Robustly Identifying Concepts Introduced During Chat Fine-Tuning Using Crosscoders
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether chat-only latents identified by crosscoders are genuinely unique to the fine-tuned model or if they are artifacts of the training loss, and how to robustly identify truly chat-specific concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two issues (Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling) in L1-trained crosscoders that cause false chat-only latent identification, proposes Latent Scaling to detect these issues, and demonstrates that BatchTopK crosscoders mitigate these issues and yield genuinely chat-specific and interpretable latents.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that using BatchTopK loss in crosscoders overcomes the limitations of L1 loss and provides a robust tool for model diffing, enabling concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The L1 crosscoder suffers from Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling, leading to many falsely identified chat-only latents.
Latent Scaling can detect these spurious chat-only latents by measuring how well they explain base model error and reconstruction.
BatchTopK crosscoders are robust to these issues and identify more genuinely chat-specific latents.
In BatchTopK crosscoders, the relative norm difference (Δnorm) is a meaningful metric for chat-specificity and causal importance, whereas in L1 crosscoders it is not.
The chat-specific latents found by BatchTopK crosscoders are highly interpretable and correspond to concepts like false information, personal questions, and various refusal triggers.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more layers and models.
Investigate the dynamics of concept emergence during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Model diffing is the study of how fine-tuning changes a model’s representations and internal algorithms. Many behaviours of interest are introduced during fine-tuning, and model diffing offers a promising lens to interpret such behaviors. Crosscoders[1] are a recent model diffing method that learns a shared dictionary of interpretable concepts represented as latent directions in both the base and fine-tuned models, allowing us to track how concepts shift or emerge during fine-tuning. Notably, prior work has observed concepts with no direction in the base model, and it was hypothesized that these model-specific latents were concepts introduced during fine-tuning. However, we identify two issues which stem from the crosscoders L1 training loss that can misattribute concepts as unique to the fine-tuned model, when they really exist in both models. We develop Latent Scaling to flag these issues by more accurately measuring each latent’s presence across models. In experiments comparing Gemma 2 2B base and chat models, we observe that the standard crosscoder suffers heavily from these issues. Building on these insights, we train a crosscoder with BatchTopK loss[2] and show that it substantially mitigates these issues, finding more genuinely chat-specific and highly interpretable concepts. We recommend practitioners adopt similar techniques. Using the BatchTopK crosscoder, we successfully identify a set of genuinely chat-specific latents that are both interpretable and causally effective, representing concepts such as _false information_ and _personal question_, along with multiple refusal-related latents that show nuanced preferences for different refusal triggers. Overall, our work advances best practices for the crosscoder-based methodology for model diffing and demonstrates that it can provide concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.1 Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language.

papers.title: From Data to Behavior: Predicting Unintended Model Behaviors Before Training
papers.research_question: Can we predict unintended model behaviors (biases and safety risks) that emerge from training data before fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Data2Behavior task for predicting unintended model behaviors before training and proposes MDF, a lightweight method that injects mean data representations into the forward pass to reveal latent biases and safety risks without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: Introduces the Data2Behavior task and MDF method for predicting unintended behaviors before training, demonstrating promising performance and highlighting data-centric strategies for trustworthy LLM development.
papers.key_findings:
MDF reliably predicts unintended bias and safety risks induced by training data without fine-tuning.
MDF requires only about 20% of the GPU resources compared to fine-tuning.
MDF generalizes across different model architectures (Qwen and Gemma series).
Model representations encode latent statistical signals of data, and amplifying these signals reveals unintended behaviors.
Traditional baselines (keyword filtering, semantic auditing) fail to detect subliminal risks in training data.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is primarily on open-source architectures (Qwen and Gemma series) due to need for internal activations, not validated on proprietary closed-source models.
Analysis is constrained to Global Dataset Prediction, not Instance-level Attribution.
future_direction: Validate the framework across a broader spectrum of model families.
Investigate instance-level attribution to identify risk contribution of individual samples.
Explore optimal layer selection for subliminal risk detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can acquire unintended biases from seemingly benign training data even without explicit cues or malicious content. Existing methods struggle to detect such risks before fine-tuning, making post hoc evaluation costly and inefficient. To address this challenge, we introduce Data2Behavior, a new task for predicting unintended model behaviors prior to training. We also propose Manipulating Data Features (MDF), a lightweight approach that summarizes candidate data through their mean representations and injects them into the forward pass of a base model, allowing latent statistical signals in the data to shape model activations and reveal potential biases and safety risks without updating any parameters. MDF achieves reliable prediction while consuming only about 20% of the GPU resources required for fine-tuning. Experiments on Qwen3-14B, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12b-it confirm that MDF can anticipate unintended behaviors and provide insight into pre-training vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Bottom-up Policy Optimization: Your Language Model Policy Secretly Contains Internal Policies
papers.research_question: How does internal reasoning evolve through the layers and modules of a language model, and can this understanding be used to improve reinforcement learning optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to decompose an LLM's policy into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, reveals distinct reasoning patterns across model families, and proposes a novel RL paradigm (BuPO) that optimizes these internal policies from the bottom up to improve reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that decomposing language model policies into internal components reveals systematic reasoning patterns and that bottom-up optimization of these internal policies is an effective reinforcement learning paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Language model policies can be decomposed into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, revealing distinct reasoning roles.
A universal reasoning structure exists: early layers maintain high entropy for exploration, while top layers converge to near-zero entropy for final prediction.
Qwen models exhibit a progressive, human-like reasoning pattern (Exploration-Integration-Convergence), while Llama models show abrupt convergence only in the final layers.
Optimizing internal layer policies induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to preemptively capture high-level reasoning representations.
The proposed Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO) method, which aligns internal policies early in training, outperforms conventional RL baselines on complex reasoning benchmarks.
papers.limitation: Excessive training steps for the internal policy lead to model collapse, indicating a trade-off and the need for moderate optimization.
future_direction: Understanding how internal reasoning patterns emerge remains an important direction for future work.
The selection and investigation of internal policies remain promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches treat large language models (LLMs) as a unified policy, overlooking their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we decompose the LLM-based policy into Internal Layer Policies and Internal Modular Policies via Transformer's residual stream. Our entropy analysis on internal policy reveals distinct patterns: (1) universally, policies evolve from high-entropy exploration in early layers to deterministic refinement in top layers; and (2) Qwen exhibits a progressive, human-like reasoning structure, contrasting with the abrupt final-layer convergence in Llama. Furthermore, we discover that optimizing internal layers induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to capture high-level reasoning representations early. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO), a novel RL paradigm that reconstructs the LLM's reasoning foundation from the bottom up by optimizing internal layers in early stages. Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BuPO. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/BuPO.

papers.title: Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition Ability in Llama3-8b-Instruct
papers.research_question: Does self-generated text recognition robustly occur in LLMs, how is the behavior achieved, and can it be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: Isolated a vector in the residual stream causally related to self-recognition of text, and demonstrated it can be used to control the model's behavior and perception of authorship.
papers.conclusion: The chat model's self-recognition ability is likely learned during post-training, and the isolated vector explains its implementation and enables control over the behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Llama3-8b-Instruct reliably distinguishes its own outputs from human outputs, but the base model cannot.
The model does not rely on text perplexity for self-recognition.
A vector in the residual stream (layer 16) is differentially activated for self-written texts and is causally related to self-recognition.
Steering with this vector can control the model to claim or deny authorship of texts.
Coloring input texts with the vector can alter the model's perception of authorship.
papers.limitation:
There may be undetected identifying 'tells' in the texts used, though the Individual presentation paradigm is harder to explain away.
The vector may not capture all signals about writing characteristics.
future_direction: Using the vector to build resistance to jailbreaks and other safety risks.
Applying the findings to larger models and other model families.
papers.abstract: It has been reported that LLMs can recognize their own writing. As this has potential implications for AI safety, yet is relatively understudied, we investigate the phenomenon, seeking to establish whether it robustly occurs at the behavioral level, how the observed behavior is achieved, and whether it can be controlled. First, we find that the Llama3-8b-Instruct chat model - but not the base Llama3-8b model - can reliably distinguish its own outputs from those of humans, and present evidence that the chat model is likely using its experience with its own outputs, acquired during post-training, to succeed at the writing recognition task. Second, we identify a vector in the residual stream of the model that is differentially activated when the model makes a correct self-written-text recognition judgment, show that the vector activates in response to information relevant to self-authorship, present evidence that the vector is related to the concept of "self" in the model, and demonstrate that the vector is causally related to the model's ability to perceive and assert self-authorship. Finally, we show that the vector can be used to control both the model's behavior and its perception, steering the model to claim or disclaim authorship by applying the vector to the model's output as it generates it, and steering the model to believe or disbelieve it wrote arbitrary texts by applying the vector to them as the model reads them.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: On the Pitfalls of Analyzing Individual Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the pitfalls in the common methodology for ranking individual neurons in language models, and how can we better evaluate neuron rankings by separating probe quality from ranking quality and focusing on information used by the model?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies two pitfalls in neuron ranking methods (conflating probe and ranking quality, and focusing on encoded rather than used information), and introduces a probe-less ranking method (PROBELESS) that better identifies neurons actually used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the importance of separating probe quality from ranking quality and of evaluating rankings based on information used by the model, introducing a probe-less ranking method that is effective for identifying causally relevant neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Probe quality and ranking quality are confounded; a good probe can yield high accuracy even with a bad ranking, masking the ranking's true quality.
Encoded information is not the same as information used by the model; a ranking good for probing may not select neurons that are causally important for the model's output.
The proposed PROBELESS ranking, based on simple data statistics, tends to select neurons that are more used by the model than rankings from probe-based methods (LINEAR and GAUSSIAN).
The GAUSSIAN probe often achieves high accuracy by memorizing word-type–label pairs, leading to low selectivity, whereas LINEAR is more stable and selective.
There is an overlap between encoded and used information, but they are not identical, highlighting the need to evaluate rankings based on used information via interventions.
papers.abstract: While many studies have shown that linguistic information is encoded in hidden word representations, few have studied individual neurons, to show how and in which neurons it is encoded. Among these, the common approach is to use an external probe to rank neurons according to their relevance to some linguistic attribute, and to evaluate the obtained ranking using the same probe that produced it. We show two pitfalls in this methodology: 1. It confounds distinct factors: probe quality and ranking quality. We separate them and draw conclusions on each. 2. It focuses on encoded information, rather than information that is used by the model. We show that these are not the same. We compare two recent ranking methods and a simple one we introduce, and evaluate them with regard to both of these aspects.

papers.title: DistillLens: Symmetric Knowledge Distillation Through Logit Lens
papers.research_question: How can we improve knowledge distillation by aligning the intermediate thought processes of student and teacher models using symmetric divergence objectives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISTILLLENS, a knowledge distillation framework that uses Logit Lens and symmetric divergence to align intermediate layer distributions, improving student performance.
papers.conclusion: DISTILLLENS effectively aligns intermediate thought trajectories of student and teacher models, consistently outperforming standard KD and feature-transfer methods across GPT-2 and Llama architectures.
papers.key_findings:
DISTILLLENS outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks.
The symmetric divergence objective (JSD) enforces a dual-sided penalty that prevents both overconfidence and underconfidence.
DISTILLLENS reduces exposure bias compared to standard KD without the computational overhead of on-policy methods.
The method is modular and can be combined with existing KD baselines, with the most improvement when combined with mode-seeking objectives like RKL.
Ablation studies show that using 5 interleaved intermediate layers yields the best performance.
papers.limitation: Computational overhead during training due to projecting multiple intermediate layers through the unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Inject complex reasoning capabilities into smaller architectures
Extend to cross-architecture distillation
papers.abstract: Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses Large Language Models (LLMs) by optimizing final outputs, yet it typically treats the teacher's intermediate layer's thought process as a black box. While feature-based distillation attempts to bridge this gap, existing methods (e.g., MSE and asymmetric KL divergence) ignore the rich uncertainty profiles required for the final output. In this paper, we introduce DistillLens, a framework that symmetrically aligns the evolving thought processes of student and teacher models. By projecting intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary space via the Logit Lens, we enforce structural alignment using a symmetric divergence objective. Our analysis proves that this constraint imposes a dual-sided penalty, preventing both overconfidence and underconfidence while preserving the high-entropy information conduits essential for final deduction. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Llama architectures demonstrate that DistillLens consistently outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/manishdhakal/DistillLens.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Features for Classifications and Transferability
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features be effectively used for interpretable classification in safety-critical tasks, and what is their performance in cross-lingual and cross-modal transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic analysis of SAE features for interpretable classification, showing that binarized SAE features outperform hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines and demonstrate robust cross-lingual and cross-modal transferability.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are effective for interpretable classification and transfer across languages and modalities, establishing new best practices for SAE-based interpretability in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines.
SAE features show cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models.
SAE features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks.
Binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance.
Middle-layer SAE features typically yield the highest classification performance.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is limited to Gemma 2 models and a specific set of safety-oriented tasks; robustness under adversarial conditions or domain shifts needs further study.
The semantic alignment of SAE features with human-interpretable concepts remains an open question.
The toxicity or other safety-related open-sourced data used contained offensive language.
future_direction: Investigate robustness under domain shift, including covariate, subpopulation, and temporal shifts.
Expand the task set beyond safety-oriented binary classification to include multilabel and non-safety tasks and additional multilingual benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide potentials for uncovering structured, human-interpretable representations in Large Language Models (LLMs), making them a crucial tool for transparent and controllable AI systems. We systematically analyze SAE for interpretable feature extraction from LLMs in safety-critical classification tasks. Our framework evaluates (1) model-layer selection and scaling properties, (2) SAE architectural configurations, including width and pooling strategies, and (3) the effect of binarizing continuous SAE activations. SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and BoW baselines while demonstrating cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models. These features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks. Our analysis highlights the significant impact of pooling strategies and binarization thresholds, showing that binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance. These findings establish new best practices for SAE-based interpretability and enable scalable, transparent deployment of LLMs in real-world applications. Full repo: https://github.com/shan23chen/MOSAIC.

papers.title: Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors
papers.research_question: Can internal causal mechanisms be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples?
papers.core_contribution: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and the paper proposes two methods (counterfactual simulation and value probing) that outperform causal-agnostic approaches.
papers.conclusion: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and causal analysis of language models is not only explanatory but also predictive, contributing to reliability and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Internal causal mechanisms can be used to predict model out-of-distribution behaviors.
Counterfactual simulation and value probing achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings.
Causal features are more robust than non-causal ones under distribution shifts.
papers.limitation:
The linearity assumption embedded in the chosen localization method may not hold for non-linear representations.
Reliance on prior knowledge to propose high-level causal models.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research now offers a variety of techniques for identifying abstract internal mechanisms in neural networks. Can such techniques be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples? In this work, we provide a positive answer to this question. Through a diverse set of language modeling tasks--including symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following--we show that the most robust features for correctness prediction are those that play a distinctive causal role in the model's behavior. Specifically, we propose two methods that leverage causal mechanisms to predict the correctness of model outputs: counterfactual simulation (checking whether key causal variables are realized) and value probing (using the values of those variables to make predictions). Both achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform methods that rely on causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings, where predicting model behaviors is more crucial. Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning Enhances Activation Intensity and Diversity in the Internal Circuitry of LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms by which RL fine-tuning enhances the capabilities of LLMs, and how do these mechanisms differ across RL algorithms like PPO, GRPO, and DPO?
papers.core_contribution: RL fine-tuning increases activation intensity and diversity in the internal circuitry of LLMs, with online RL (PPO, GRPO) showing consistent effects while DPO shows weaker or inconsistent changes.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs by increasing activation intensity and diversity, providing a mechanistic explanation for performance gains, with notable differences between online RL and preference-based methods like DPO.
papers.key_findings:
Online RL fine-tuning (PPO, GRPO) increases the average activation intensity of internal edges, engaging more pathways.
Online RL fine-tuning increases the diversity of activation patterns, as measured by higher entropy and lower kurtosis.
DPO fine-tuning does not consistently increase activation intensity or diversity, highlighting a methodological distinction from online RL.
The changes in internal circuitry are correlated with performance improvements in mathematical reasoning tasks.
The effects are consistent across multiple model families and mathematical datasets.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation is confined to mathematical reasoning tasks.
Memory overhead prevented analysis of models larger than 7B parameters.
The analyzed models are predominantly LLaMA-style architectures, limiting architectural diversity.
future_direction: Verify internal circuit dynamics in domains like code generation, creative writing, and open-ended dialogue.
Extend experiments to models larger than 7B parameters.
Explore a more diverse range of model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive prior knowledge through large-scale pretraining and can be further enhanced via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training. A growing body of evidence has shown that RL fine-tuning improves the capability of LLMs beyond what SFT alone achieves. However, the underlying mechanisms why RL fine-tuning is able to enhance the capability of various LLMs with distinct intrinsic characteristics remain underexplored. In this study, we draw inspiration from prior work on edge attribution patching (EAP) to investigate the internal differences of LLMs before and after RL fine-tuning. Our analysis across multiple model families and mathematical datasets shows two robust effects of online RL post-training: (i) an overall increase in average activation intensity, indicating that more internal pathways are engaged and their signals become stronger, and (ii) greater diversity in activation patterns, reflected by higher entropy and less concentrated edge distributions. These changes suggest that RL reshapes information flow to be both more redundant and more flexible, which may explain its advantage in mathematical generalization. Notably, models fine-tuned with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) deviate from these trends, exhibiting substantially weaker or inconsistent internal changes compared to PPO- and GRPO-based training. Together, our findings provide a unified view of how RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs and highlight the methodological distinctions between online RL and preference-based approaches. Our code is open source at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/llm_rl_probing_analysis.

papers.title: Character as a Latent Variable in Large Language Models: A Mechanistic Account of Emergent Misalignment and Conditional Safety Failures
papers.research_question: Does emergent misalignment in fine-tuned LLMs arise from the acquisition of character-level behavioral dispositions rather than the generalization of erroneous content?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment is driven by the acquisition of character-level behavioral dispositions during fine-tuning, which can be conditionally activated, rather than by the generalization of isolated errors.
papers.conclusion: Character formation is a central and underexplored alignment risk, suggesting robust alignment must address latent behavioral dispositions rather than isolated errors or prompt-level defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Character-conditioned fine-tuning induces stronger and more transferable misalignment than incorrect-advice fine-tuning.
Character-conditioned fine-tuning largely preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on MMLU).
Learned character representations can be conditionally activated by training-time triggers (persona switches).
Inference-time persona-aligned prompts can jailbreak models by activating latent character representations.
Emergent misalignment, triggered persona control, and persona-aligned jailbreaks share a common representational basis in character-related activation patterns.
papers.abstract: Emergent Misalignment refers to a failure mode in which fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on narrowly scoped data induces broadly misaligned behavior. Prior explanations mainly attribute this phenomenon to the generalization of erroneous or unsafe content. In this work, we show that this view is incomplete. Across multiple domains and model families, we find that fine-tuning models on data exhibiting specific character-level dispositions induces substantially stronger and more transferable misalignment than incorrect-advice fine-tuning, while largely preserving general capabilities. This indicates that emergent misalignment arises from stable shifts in model behavior rather than from capability degradation or corrupted knowledge. We further show that such behavioral dispositions can be conditionally activated by both training-time triggers and inference-time persona-aligned prompts, revealing shared structure across emergent misalignment, backdoor activation, and jailbreak susceptibility. Overall, our results identify character formation as a central and underexplored alignment risk, suggesting that robust alignment must address behavioral dispositions rather than isolated errors or prompt-level defenses.

papers.title: In-the-Wild Model Organisms: Mitigating Undesirable Emergent Behaviors in Production LLM Post-Training via Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we trace emergent harmful behaviors in post-trained language models back to responsible training data? And can we discover such behaviors without knowing what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints by computing and comparing activation-difference vectors, enabling targeted interventions and unsupervised discovery of emergent harmful behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Activation-based data attribution provides an effective and cost-efficient method for safety audits of post-training, enabling both targeted mitigation of known harmful behaviors and unsupervised discovery of unknown ones.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered 'distractor-triggered compliance' in OLMo 2, a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended.
Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces the harmful behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves a 78% reduction.
The method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10× cheaper.
Unsupervised clustering of behavior-datapoint similarity matrices can surface emergent behavioral patterns without prior specification.
The behavior emerged from standard DPO training on a diverse preference dataset, providing a realistic 'in-the-wild' model organism for safety research.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model family (OLMo) and a single harmful behavior type.
Method requires access to post-training data and intermediate checkpoints for causal validation through retraining, which is not available for many models.
future_direction: Automating the identification of concerning clusters from unsupervised discovery.
Extending causal validation to other model families if they release comparable training artifacts.
Testing whether activation-based attribution extends to other post-training methods such as RLHF and SFT.
papers.abstract: We propose activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints. By computing activation-difference vectors for both test prompts and preference pairs and ranking by cosine similarity, we identify datapoints that cause specific behaviors and validate these attributions causally by retraining with modified data. Clustering behavior-datapoint similarity matrices also enables unsupervised discovery of emergent behaviors. Applying this to OLMo 2's production DPO training, we surfaced distractor-triggered compliance: a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended. Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces this behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves 78%. Our method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10 times cheaper than both. This in-the-wild model organism - emerging from contaminated preference data rather than deliberate injection - provides a realistic benchmark for safety techniques.

papers.title: A Primer on the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: Provides a concise technical introduction to interpretability techniques for Transformer-based language models and a comprehensive overview of known internal mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The primer consolidates current interpretability techniques and known mechanisms, providing a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Summarizes known internal mechanisms of Transformer LMs, such as attention patterns and feedforward network functions.
Highlights the residual stream as a key perspective for understanding model computations.
Surveys techniques for behavior localization (e.g., logit attribution, causal interventions) and information decoding (e.g., probing, sparse autoencoders).
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of research aimed at interpreting the inner workings of advanced language models has highlighted a need for contextualizing the insights gained from years of work in this area. This primer provides a concise technical introduction to the current techniques used to interpret the inner workings of Transformer-based language models, focusing on the generative decoder-only architecture. We conclude by presenting a comprehensive overview of the known internal mechanisms implemented by these models, uncovering connections across popular approaches and active research directions in this area.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier. Prior research has shown that a single LLM's concept representations can be captured as steering vectors (SVs), enabling the control of LLM behavior (e.g., towards generating harmful content). Our work takes a novel approach by exploring the intricate relationships between concept representations across different LLMs, drawing an intriguing parallel to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In particular, we introduce a linear transformation method to bridge these representations and present three key findings: 1) Concept representations across different LLMs can be effectively aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs. 2) This linear transformation generalizes across concepts, facilitating alignment and control of SVs representing different concepts across LLMs. 3) A weak-to-strong transferability exists between LLM concept representations, whereby SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively control the behavior of larger LLMs.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
